title: Absolute Extrema on a Closed Interval
quickIdea: On a closed interval, evaluate f at every critical point inside and at both endpoints, then take the largest and smallest. Nothing else can be an absolute extremum.
remember: Extreme value theorem: a continuous f on a closed bounded interval [a, b] attains an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum there.
The complete candidate list is: points in (a, b) where f'(c) = 0, points in (a, b) where f' does not exist, and the two endpoints a and b.
Compare the values of f, not the values of f'. A stationary point can give the smallest value while an endpoint gives the largest.
Continuity on the closed interval is what guarantees the maximum exists; on an open interval the supremum may be approached and never reached.
If f is not continuous, the theorem fails: 1/x on (0, 1] has no minimum, and a jump function on [0, 1] can miss its supremum.

example.prompt: GATE CSE 1997 Q.4.1: what is the maximum value of f(x) = 2x^2 - 2x + 6 on [0, 2]?
example.work: f'(x) = 4x - 2 vanishes at x = 1/2, the only critical point. Values: f(0) = 6, f(1/2) = 0.5 - 1 + 6 = 5.5, f(2) = 8 - 4 + 6 = 10. The largest of the three is 10.
example.answer: The maximum value is 10, attained at the endpoint x = 2. The stationary point gives the minimum, 5.5.

gateAngle: 1997 Q.4.1 is the pure closed-interval question, and its trap is the one the MIT lecture warns about: solving f'(x) = 0 alone returns the minimum and you report the opposite of the truth. Any GATE question that says 'in the interval [a, b]' is asking for this candidate list.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 1997 Q.4.1: the maximum value of 2x^2 - 2x + 6 on [0, 2].
variations.why: The endpoint, not the stationary point, supplies the maximum.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Find the absolute maximum and minimum of f(x) = x^3 - 3x on [0, 3].
variations.answer: Maximum 18 at x = 3, minimum -2 at x = 1. Candidates: f(0) = 0, f(1) = -2, f(3) = 18; the critical point x = -1 is outside the interval and is not a candidate.
variations.why: Adds the second half of the discipline: a critical point outside the interval must be discarded before comparing.

trap.what: Answering with the value at the stationary point because it is the only point the derivative found.
trap.why: The derivative is blind to endpoints, and on a closed interval the largest value is very often at one of them.
trap.counterexample: On [0, 2], f(x) = 2x^2 - 2x + 6 is 5.5 at its only stationary point and 10 at x = 2. MIT's wire-into-squares example fails the other way: there the stationary point is the minimum while the largest value sits at the ends.

check.question: f(x) = x^4 - 4x on [0, 2]. Where are the absolute extrema?
check.answer: Minimum -3 at x = 1, maximum 8 at x = 2.
check.explanation: f'(x) = 4x^3 - 4 vanishes at x = 1 only. f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1 - 4 = -3, f(2) = 16 - 8 = 8, so the endpoint gives the maximum.
